The Greater European peaclam Pisidium amnicum exhibits a shell length at emergence of 0.22 centimeters , a dimension that positions its neonates among the smallest recorded for sphaeriid bivalves. Newly released juveniles are barely discernible to the naked eye, and their initial growth trajectory relies heavily on the nutrient-rich marsupial environment provided by the parent. Comparative estimates derived from the congener Sphaerium corneum suggest a shell length at emergence of approximately 0.006 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.006 centimeters], though direct observations for P. amnicum remain limited due to the technical challenge of isolating individual newborn clams from the brood chamber without causing damage. This minuscule initial size imposes a steep energetic challenge during the early post-release phase, as the juveniles must begin filter-feeding almost immediately upon emergence into the benthic substrate. Field surveys consistently indicate that the fine gravel and sand of well-oxygenated rivers provide the interstitial refuge necessary for these minute bivalves to avoid displacement and predation during their most vulnerable period.

Sexual maturation in Pisidium amnicum, as in many sphaeriid clams, is tightly coupled to the attainment of a specific shell dimension rather than a strict chronological age. Longitudinal growth studies confirm that the shell length at puberty is 0.456 centimeters [Lp = 0.456 centimeters], a threshold at which the developing gonad initiates gametogenesis and the brood pouch becomes structurally competent to incubate fertilized ova. Individuals that reach this size during the early summer months typically spawn within the same reproductive season, whereas those achieving it late in the autumn may delay their first reproductive effort until the following spring. The onset of reproductive capability marks a critical transition in the species' life history, after which energy allocation shifts substantially to accommodate the simultaneous demands of somatic growth and embryonic brooding. This dual investment is reflected in the comparatively modest ultimate dry weight recorded for the species, which under controlled laboratory conditions reaches 0.091 grams , a value that aligns closely with predictions based on shell length to ash-free dry weight regressions developed for the related species Pisidium casertanum.

At a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], total fecundity across the entire adult lifespan of the Greater European peaclam reaches 260 offspring , a figure that integrates both the modest clutch size and the extended reproductive tenure characteristic of the species. Females produce between 3 and 37 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = between 3 and 37 eggs per reproductive event], and they may complete anywhere from 5 to 41 such brooding cycles over the course of their lives [F_R_i = 5 to 41 such brooding cycles over the course of their lives]. The pronounced variability in both clutch size and brooding frequency reflects phenotypic plasticity in response to local food availability and the energetic condition of the gravid adult. Individuals inhabiting nutrient-rich, silt-laden reaches of lowland rivers tend to exhibit both larger brood sizes and a greater number of successive broods compared to those occupying oligotrophic headwater streams, where reproductive output is more constrained.

Under controlled conditions maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan reaches 518.5 days [am = 518.5 days], a duration that permits the accumulation of several successive broods. This relatively slow pace of life is consistent with the species' cold-water, stable-habitat preferences, where metabolic rates are dampened and extrinsic mortality from predation is relatively low. Field-based studies that track marked individuals through seasonal recapture events often report this longevity as approximately 17 months [am = approximately 17 months] at the same temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The congruence between captive and field estimates supports the conclusion that physiological senescence rather than environmental stochasticity is the primary determinant of lifespan in this species, although summer temperature extremes can accelerate age-related deterioration in marginal populations.

The ultimate shell height of Pisidium amnicum, representing the maximum recorded dimension of the adult valve, has been documented at 1.66 centimeters [Li = 1.66 centimeters], a measurement that establishes this species as one of the larger members of its genus within Palearctic freshwater systems. This asymptotic size is achieved gradually over the full course of the animal's life, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity as resources are partitioned between continued somatic expansion and the energetic costs of brooding. Field collections from the River Thames system have yielded specimens approaching this maximum dimension predominantly in stable, low-velocity reaches where silt deposition provides a rich source of organic particulates. The species' ultimate dry weight, recorded at 0.091 grams , is modest in absolute terms but represents a more than thousand-fold increase over the mass of a newly emerged juvenile, underscoring the substantial cumulative investment in somatic tissue over the prolonged lifespan. Comparisons with smaller congeners such as Pisidium casertanum highlight the allometric relationship that constrains maximum shell height against the mechanical limitations of the hinge ligament and adductor musculature.
